theory.what: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a 7-layer conceptual framework that standardizes how network communication works across different systems and technologies. Developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in 1984, it remains the primary reference model for teaching and troubleshooting networks worldwide. Each layer has a specific function and communicates only with its peer layer on the receiving device, creating a modular architecture where changes in one layer do not require changes in others.
theory.why: Understanding the OSI model is fundamental because it provides a common language for troubleshooting across teams and technologies. When something breaks, you can isolate which layer is failing — is it a physical cable issue (Layer 1), a switching problem (Layer 2), a routing issue (Layer 3), or an application bug (Layer 7)? This layered approach means a web developer diagnosing a timeout doesn't need to know the intricacies of Ethernet frame structure, and a cabling technician doesn't need to understand HTTP status codes. In practice, seasoned network engineers use the OSI model instinctively: a customer reports 'the internet is down,' and they mentally walk through the layers — is the link light on (L1)? Can I ping the gateway (L3)? Does DNS resolve (L7)? Without this mental framework, troubleshooting becomes random guesswork.
theory.how:
Data flows down the stack on the sender (encapsulation) and up the stack on the receiver (de-encapsulation). Each layer adds its own header with control information:

| Layer | Name | Example Protocols | Data Unit | Function |
|-------|------|-----------------|-----------|----------|
| 7 | Application | HTTP, DNS, SMTP | Data | User-facing services |
| 6 | Presentation | TLS, SSL, JPEG | Data | Encryption, compression, translation |
| 5 | Session | NetBIOS, RPC | Data | Session management, checkpoints |
| 4 | Transport | TCP, UDP | Segment/Datagram | End-to-end delivery, reliability |
| 3 | Network | IP, ICMP, OSPF | Packet | Logical addressing, routing |
| 2 | Data Link | Ethernet, Wi-Fi | Frame | MAC addressing, framing, error detection |
| 1 | Physical | Cables, radio | Bits | Raw bit transmission |

A useful mnemonic from bottom to top: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application). The key insight: each layer believes it is speaking directly to its counterpart on the other device. Layer 4 thinks it talks to Layer 4, but in reality, data must physically travel down and back up the stack.
theory.when: Use the OSI model in three key scenarios: (1) Troubleshooting — start from Layer 1 (is the cable plugged in?) and work up methodically. Check physical connectivity first — a surprising number of 'network is down' tickets are solved by reseating a cable. Then verify Layer 2 (switching), Layer 3 (routing), Layer 4 (firewalls), and finally Layer 7 (application config). (2) Network design — when architecting a new network, the OSI layers help you think about which devices and protocols belong at each layer. (3) Communication — when describing a network problem to a colleague, referencing the layer ('I'm seeing an issue at Layer 2') instantly conveys the scope and eliminates whole categories of possible causes.
key_concepts: Encapsulation — each layer wraps the data from the layer above
PDU (Protocol Data Unit) — the generic term for data at any layer
Each layer serves the layer above it and is served by the layer below
Layers 1-4 = transport mechanisms, Layers 5-7 = application support
Peer-to-peer communication — each layer talks logically to its counterpart
Modularity — changing one layer doesn't require changing others
theory.configuration: N/A — conceptual model, not a configurable protocol
troubleshooting: Layer 1: Check cables, link lights, interface status, power supplies
Layer 2: Check MAC table, ARP cache, VLAN assignment, STP state
Layer 3: Check IP config, routing table, ping, traceroute
Layer 4: Check port connectivity, firewall rules, TCP handshake
Layer 5: Check session timeouts, load balancer persistence
Layer 6: Check certificate validity, encryption mismatches
Layer 7: Check application logs, DNS resolution, HTTP status codes

theory.what: The TCP/IP model is a 4-layer practical networking model that the internet actually uses. Developed by the US Department of Defense through DARPA research in the 1970s, it predates the OSI model and was designed for a fundamentally different purpose: resilient communication across a decentralized, packet-switched network that could survive nuclear attack. Unlike OSI which was designed first as a standard and implemented later, TCP/IP grew from real implementations (the ARPANET) into a standard — which is why it's simpler, more pragmatic, and maps directly to real protocols running today.
theory.why: While OSI is theoretical, TCP/IP is what actually runs the internet. Every packet you send — every email, every web request, every streaming video — uses this model from the moment it leaves your device until it arrives at its destination. Understanding TCP/IP means understanding how data flows across the global internet: how your browser knows to use TCP for reliable page loads but your video call uses UDP for speed; how your packet finds its way across continents; how a router knows where to forward data. Without this foundation, advanced networking concepts like routing protocols, firewalls, and traffic engineering remain impenetrable.
theory.how:
The TCP/IP model has 4 layers that map loosely to OSI:

| Layer | OSI Equivalent | Examples | Function |
|-------|----------------|----------|----------|
| Application | 5-7 (Session/Pres/App) | HTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTP, FTP | User services, data formatting |
| Transport | 4 | TCP, UDP | End-to-end reliability, flow control |
| Internet | 3 | IP, ICMP, ARP | Addressing, routing, packet forwarding |
| Network Access | 1-2 | Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP | Physical transmission, framing |

Data flow example — loading a web page:
1. **Application**: Browser sends HTTP GET request
2. **Transport**: TCP segments the request, assigns source/dest ports (80), adds sequence numbers
3. **Internet**: IP wraps each segment in a packet with source/dest IP addresses
4. **Network Access**: Ethernet frames the packet with MAC addresses and sends it as bits on the wire

The receiving device reverses the process: bits → frame → packet → segment → HTTP response.
theory.when: Use TCP/IP for all real-world networking discussions and implementations. OSI is best for conceptual teaching and structured troubleshooting. Key distinction: an OSI purist might say 'Layer 3 problem'; a TCP/IP practitioner says 'routing issue' and reaches for ping/traceroute. When configuring devices, writing firewall rules, or analyzing packet captures, you're working in TCP/IP terms. The OSI-to-TCP/IP mapping is: OSI 5-7 → TCP/IP Application, OSI 4 → Transport, OSI 3 → Internet, OSI 1-2 → Network Access.
key_concepts: 4 layers vs OSI's 7 — more practical, less abstract
IP is connectionless (best-effort delivery — packets can be lost)
TCP provides reliability through sequencing and acknowledgments
UDP provides speed with no reliability guarantees
The 'hourglass' design — IP at the narrow waist connects everything
theory.configuration:
# Linux
ip addr add 192.168.1.1/24 dev eth0
ip route add default via 192.168.1.254

# Cisco
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
troubleshooting: ping (ICMP — tests Internet layer connectivity)
traceroute (path discovery — maps each hop)
netstat/ss (Transport layer connection state)
nslookup/dig (Application layer — DNS resolution)
tcpdump (packet capture — inspect all layers)

theory.what: Subnetting divides a large network into smaller, more manageable sub-networks (subnets). Each subnet has its own network address (all host bits 0), broadcast address (all host bits 1), and a range of usable host addresses in between. At its core, subnetting is about borrowing bits from the host portion of an IP address and reassigning them as network bits, which increases the number of networks available while reducing the number of hosts per network.
theory.why: Without subnetting, you'd have one massive broadcast domain where every device sees every other device's broadcast traffic. In a network of 500 devices, ARP broadcasts alone would consume significant bandwidth. Subnetting solves this by: (1) reducing broadcast traffic — broadcasts are contained within each subnet; (2) improving security — different subnets can be separated by firewalls; (3) enabling efficient IP allocation — give each department only what it needs; (4) enabling routing — routers move traffic between subnets. In enterprise networking, subnetting is the foundation of VLAN design, routing policies, and security segmentation.
theory.how:
Subnetting works by extending the subnet mask to borrow bits from the host portion. Each borrowed bit doubles the number of subnets but halves the available hosts.

**Worked Example — Splitting a /24 into 4 subnets:**
Given network 192.168.1.0/24 (255.255.255.0):
• To get 4 subnets, we need 2 subnet bits (2^2 = 4)
• New mask: /26 (255.255.255.192)
• Each subnet has 6 host bits → 2^6 - 2 = 62 usable hosts

| Subnet | Network Address | Usable Range | Broadcast |
|--------|----------------|--------------|-----------|
| 1 | 192.168.1.0/26 | .1 – .62 | .63 |
| 2 | 192.168.1.64/26 | .65 – .126 | .127 |
| 3 | 192.168.1.128/26 | .129 – .190 | .191 |
| 4 | 192.168.1.192/26 | .193 – .254 | .255 |

**Key formulas:**
• Number of subnets = 2^n (n = borrowed bits)
• Usable hosts per subnet = 2^h - 2 (h = remaining host bits)
• Magic number = 256 - subnet mask value in the borrowed octet
  (e.g., /26 = 192, magic number = 256 - 192 = 64 → subnets increment by 64)
theory.when: Subnet when you need to: (1) separate departments or tenants — Finance doesn't need to see IoT traffic; (2) create VLANs — each VLAN maps to a subnet; (3) optimize routing — smaller routing tables with summarization; (4) meet security requirements — PCI DSS requires CDE isolation, which means separate subnets; (5) conserve IP space — a /30 (2 usable hosts) is perfect for point-to-point links. **Common mistake**: giving a point-to-point link a /24 wastes 252 IPs. A /30 or /31 is correct.
key_concepts: CIDR notation (/24, /26, /30) — shorthand for subnet mask
Network address (all host bits = 0) — identifies the subnet
Broadcast address (all host bits = 1) — sends to all hosts in subnet
Usable hosts = 2^h - 2 (subtract network and broadcast)
Magic number technique: 256 - mask value = subnet increment
VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masks) — different-sized subnets in same network
theory.configuration:
! Cisco — two subnets on one router
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description Engineering subnet
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.192
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description Marketing subnet
 ip address 192.168.1.65 255.255.255.192
!
! Verify with routing table
show ip route | include 192.168.1
troubleshooting: Hosts can't communicate? Check if they're on the same subnet (same network address)
Wrong subnet mask = wrong broadcast domain = can't reach devices outside expected range
Use 'ipcalc 192.168.1.0/26' or 'sipcalc' to verify calculations
Ping the gateway first — if that fails, it's usually a subnet mask mismatch
Check that the subnet mask is consistent across all devices in the same VLAN

theory.what: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (google.com) into IP addresses (142.250.80.46). It's often described as 'the phone book of the internet,' but that undersells it — DNS is a distributed, hierarchical, and remarkably resilient database that handles billions of queries daily. Every time you open a website, send an email, or use an API, DNS is the first step. Without DNS, you'd need to memorize IP addresses for every service you use — impractical for humans and impossible at internet scale.
theory.why: DNS matters because it's the invisible dependency of virtually every network transaction. When it breaks, everything feels broken — websites don't load, email stops flowing, APIs return errors. But DNS is also a powerful tool: (1) **Load balancing** — a single domain can resolve to multiple IPs (round-robin DNS), spreading traffic across servers; (2) **Failover** — DNS can be updated to point to backup servers during outages; (3) **CDN integration** — content delivery networks use DNS to route users to the nearest edge server; (4) **Service discovery** — microservices find each other through DNS. In enterprise networks, understanding DNS is critical because DNS issues are among the most common causes of application outages.
theory.how:
**Full resolution process (user types google.com):**
1. Browser checks its local cache — hit? Return IP immediately
2. OS checks the hosts file (/etc/hosts or C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts)
3. OS checks the local DNS resolver cache (systemd-resolved or dnscache)
4. Query sent to configured recursive resolver (ISP, 8.8.8.8, or internal DNS server)
5. Resolver walks the hierarchy: Root servers → .com TLD servers → google.com authoritative
6. Authoritative nameserver returns the A or AAAA record
7. Result cached at each level according to the TTL (Time to Live)

**Key record types:**
| Record | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| A | Maps domain to IPv4 | google.com → 142.250.80.46 |
| AAAA | Maps domain to IPv6 | google.com → 2607:f8b0::... |
| CNAME | Alias (domain → another domain) | www → example.com |
| MX | Mail server | @example.com → mail.example.com |
| NS | Authoritative nameserver | example.com → ns1.cloudflare.com |
| TXT | Arbitrary text (SPF, DKIM, verification) | SPF record: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com |
| SOA | Start of Authority — zone metadata | Primary NS, admin email, refresh timers |
theory.when: DNS is involved in virtually every network connection. Troubleshoot DNS when: (1) websites don't load but you can ping their IP — classic DNS failure symptom; (2) email delivery fails — MX records misconfigured; (3) internal services can't resolve each other — split-horizon DNS or missing internal zones; (4) after a domain transfer or NS change — propagation delay. **Common mistake**: forgetting that changes to authoritative DNS records may take up to 48 hours to fully propagate due to TTL caching. Always lower the TTL before making changes.
key_concepts: Recursive resolver (does the work for clients) vs Authoritative server (has the actual records)
TTL (Time to Live) — controls how long records are cached; lower = faster updates, more queries
DNS hierarchy: Root (.) → TLD (.com) → Authoritative (google.com)
Forward lookup (name → IP) vs Reverse lookup (IP → name via PTR records)
Split-horizon DNS — different answers for internal vs external queries
theory.configuration:
# Linux DNS client config (/etc/resolv.conf)
nameserver 8.8.8.8
nameserver 8.8.4.4
search example.com

# Windows (command line)
netsh interface ip set dns "Ethernet" static 8.8.8.8

# BIND zone file example (authoritative)
$ORIGIN example.com.
@    IN  SOA   ns1.example.com. admin.example.com. (
               2024061401 ; serial
               3600       ; refresh
               900        ; retry
               604800     ; expire
               86400      ; minimum TTL
              )
@    IN  NS    ns1.example.com.
@    IN  A     192.168.1.10
www  IN  A     192.168.1.10
mail IN  MX 10 mail.example.com.
troubleshooting: nslookup example.com — basic resolution test
dig example.com +trace — full resolution path step by step
dig @8.8.8.8 example.com — bypass local resolver, query Google's directly
dig -x 8.8.8.8 — reverse DNS lookup
Check /etc/resolv.conf or network adapter DNS settings
Flush DNS cache: sudo systemd-resolve --flush-caches (Linux) or ipconfig /flushdns (Windows)
